fully simplifying each term.

$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{8x-y^2}{2xy+3}$ oe A1

A1: $y^2x$ differentiated correctly
A1: $3y\to3\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $4x^2+k\to8x$
dM1: Make $\frac{dy}{dx}$ the subject with correct terms factored (but allow e.g. sign errors rearranging or slips in copying). There must be at least two $\frac{dy}{dx}$ terms in their expression.
A1: Correct expression, accept any equivalent.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The point $P(p,2)$, where $p$ is a constant, lies on $C$.
Given that $P$ is the minimum turning point on $C$,
(b) find
(i) the value of $p$
(ii) the value of $k$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\frac{dy}{dx}=0\Rightarrow 8x-4=0\Rightarrow x=...$ M1
$p=\frac{1}{2}$ A1
$k=2^2\times\frac{1}{2}+3\times2-4\times\frac{1}{4}=...$ M1
$k=7$ A1
(b) Note: allow all marks in (b) from a correct numerator in (a) if the denominator is incorrect.

M1: Must have been attempting $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ to find p. Substitutes back into the curve to find k. May be scored if their numerator was in terms of x only.
A1: Correct value for k

M1: Substitutes back into the curve to find the remaining unknown or other complete method to find the other value.
A1: Correct value for the other of p and k (so both should be correct).

$\Rightarrow 4\left(p-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2-1+k-6=0$ or $b^2-4ac=16-16(k-6)$ M1
(Min, single solution)$\Rightarrow p=\frac{1}{2}$ or $16-16(k-6)=0\Rightarrow k=7$ A1
$\Rightarrow k=7-4\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2$ or $4p^2-4p+7-6=0\Rightarrow p=...$ M1
The other of $p=\frac{1}{2}$ and $k=7$ A1

questions.stem:
[Figure 2: A cone, shown in Figure 2, has]
A cone, shown in Figure 2, has
• fixed height 5 cm
• base radius $r$ cm
• slant height $l$ cm

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find an expression for $l$ in terms of $r$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $(l=)\sqrt{25+r^2}$ B1
B1: Correct expression. Accept $(l=)\sqrt{5^2+r^2}$ and isw.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Given that the base radius is increasing at a constant rate of 3 cm per minute,
(b) find the rate at which the total surface area of the cone is changing when the radius of the cone is 1.5 cm. Give your answer in $\mathrm{cm}^2$ per minute to one decimal place.
[The total surface area, S, of a cone is given by the formula $S=\pi r^2+\pi rl$]
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $(S=\pi r^2+)\pi r\sqrt{25+r^2}\Rightarrow \left(\frac{dS}{dr}=2\pi r+\right)\pi\sqrt{25+r^2}+\pi r.\frac{1}{2}(25+r^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}.2r$ M1 A1
Or $(S=\pi r^2+)\pi\sqrt{25r^2+r^4}\to \left(\frac{dS}{dr}=2\pi r+\right)\pi.\frac{1}{2}(25r^2+r^4)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(50r+4r^3)$ (M1 A1)
$\frac{dS}{dt}=\frac{dS}{dr}\times\frac{dr}{dt}=..\times3$ M1
$=81.5\,(\mathrm{cm}^2/\min)$ A1
M1: Differentiates their surface area with use of the product and chain rules on a term of the form $Kr\sqrt{\pm L\pm r^2}$ - look the form (oe) $P\sqrt{"25"+r^2}+Qr^2("25"+r^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. The base area may be missing for this mark. Alternatively they may work in terms of l and the scheme marks equivalently – see box in main scheme for the derivative in this case.
Alt: Taking r inside the square root look for $K\sqrt{25r^2+r^4}\to K.\frac{1}{2}(25r^2+r^4)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(\alpha r+\beta r^3)$
A1: Correct differentiation for the curved surface area. Need not be simplified.
Alt: With r inside the square root $\pi\sqrt{25r^2+r^4}\to \pi.\frac{1}{2}(25r^2+r^4)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times(50r+4r^3)$
M1: Applies the chain rule correctly with $\frac{dr}{dt}=3$ and their expression for $\frac{dS}{dr}$ (which may be in terms of r and l or their value for $\frac{dS}{dr}$ at r = 1.5 if they find this first). This mark is for the chain rule being applied, so their previous expressions need not have been correct. If they are working in terms of l they will need to use $\frac{dS}{dt}=\frac{dS}{dl}\times\frac{dl}{dr}\times\frac{dr}{dt}$.
A1: For awrt 81.5, do not need the units. Accept $\left(9+\frac{177\sqrt{109}}{109}\right)\pi$ oe (FYI it is 81.535404…)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $\left(S=\pi(l^2-25)\right)+\pi l\sqrt{l^2-25}\Rightarrow\left(\frac{dS}{dl}=2\pi l+\right)\pi\sqrt{l^2-25}+\pi l.\frac{1}{2}(l^2-25)^{-\frac{1}{2}}.2l$ (M1 A1)
- (b) Alt 1: $\frac{dr}{dt}=3\Rightarrow r=3t(+c)\Rightarrow S=9\pi(t(+c'))^2+3\pi(t(+c'))\sqrt{25+9(t(+c'))^2}$
$\Rightarrow\frac{dS}{dt}=18\pi(t)+3\pi\sqrt{25+9(t)^2}+3\pi(t).\frac{1}{2}\left(25+9(t)^2\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}.18(t)$
Or $\frac{dS}{dt}=18\pi(t)+3\pi.\frac{1}{2}\left(25(t)^2+9(t)^4\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times\left(50(t)+36(t)^3\right)$
where ((t) may be $(t+(c'))$ throughout) M1 A1
$r=1.5\Rightarrow t(+c')=0.5\Rightarrow\frac{dS}{dt}=...$ M1
$=81.5\,(\mathrm{cm}^2/\min)$ A1
M1: Uses $\frac{dr}{dt}=3$ and integrates to $r=3t+c$, where c may be omitted (without loss of generality the time frame can be set to t = 0 when r =0), and substitutes into the surface area formula, with their l to form an expression of the correct form and proceeds to differentiate and find $\frac{dS}{dt}$ achieving a suitable form for the curved surface area part (as per main scheme, the only difference is the constant multiples).
A1: Correct differentiation for the curved surface area. Need not be simplified. Accept equivalents and may be working to t or t +c throughout.
M1: Finds t (+ c) when r = 1.5 and substitutes into their $\frac{dS}{dt}$.
A1: For awrt 81.5, or as per main scheme.
- (b) Alt 2: $\frac{dl}{dt}=\frac{dl}{dr}\frac{dr}{dt}=3\times\frac{1}{2}(r^2+25)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times2r$ M1 A1
$S=\pi r^2+\pi rl\Rightarrow\frac{dS}{dt}=2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}+\pi\frac{dr}{dt}l+\pi r\frac{dl}{dt}$ M1
$=81.5\,(\mathrm{cm}^2/\min)$ A1

A1: Correct derivative.
M1: Uses implicit differentiation to find $\frac{dS}{dt}$ in terms of $\frac{dr}{dt}$ and $\frac{dl}{dt}$.
A1: As main scheme.

parts.text:
Use proof by contradiction to prove that the curve with equation
$y=2x+x^3+\cos x$
has no stationary points.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
$y=2x+x^3+\cos x$
Assume (there is a stationary point so) $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ for some value of x B1
So for this x $\frac{dy}{dx}=2+3x^2-\sin x$ M1
$\frac{dy}{dx}=0\Rightarrow \sin x=3x^2+2\,...2$ dM1
This is a contradiction as $|\sin x|\leqslant1$ for all x, hence the assumption is false and so the function has no stationary points. A1cso
B1: For a clear, suitable assumption with reference to $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ or implication that it means $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ at some point in their proof. Need not mention "for some x", but stating "for all x" is B0. Accept just "Assume $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$"
M1: Attempts the derivative achieving $2+3x^2\pm\sin x$
dM1: Makes progress with a correct method leading to a contradiction. E.g. set their derivative equal to 0, makes sin x the subject and deduces greater than or equal to 2. Other methods are possible, e.g. states $x^2\geqslant0$ and $\sin x\leqslant1$ and deduces $2+3x^2-\sin x\geqslant1$ (hence cannot be zero). It must be clear what the contradiction will be but allow if there are some inaccuracies in details e.g. condone if a strict inequality is used for this mark. There must be reference to both $(3)x^2...0$ and the range of $\sin x$ in some way.
Do not accept "this equation has no solutions" without proof as to why there can be no solutions.
Note: A sketch is not a proof. An algebraic approach is required, but accept verbal arguments (e.g. stating "the minimum of $2+3x^2$ is 2" and "sin x cannot exceed one" etc), which may accompany a sketch.
A1cso: Fully correct proof, with derivative correct and contradiction made clear and conclusion drawn referring back to no stationary points. All necessary details must have been given. Condone cases where strict inequalities have been given instead of unstrict ones.
